claims.text: A Zr- or Ti-based oxygen getter can scavenge oxygen above 1200°C without reacting adversely with the refractory alloy or interfering with hydride decomposition.
Zr foil or Ti powder is an optimal oxygen getter for this HfNbTaTiZr process.
Zr and Ti have sufficiently high oxygen affinity relative to the alloy constituents to act as sacrificial getters.
The hydrides decompose sequentially in the order TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, and ZrH2 during heating through 600-800°C.
A heating rate of 5-10°C/min through 600-800°C is slow enough to complete the required sequential dehydrogenation.
Homogenization at 1300-1400°C for 30-60 minutes will produce chemical homogenization and nearly full densification.
An Ar atmosphere with a Zr or Ti getter can maintain oxygen below 1 ppm during sintering.
The elevated configurational entropy of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr stabilizes a disordered BCC phase at high temperature.
Hydrogen released by hydride decomposition can act as a transient interstitial phase stabilizer before being removed.
Removing residual oxygen prevents formation of oxygen-stabilized alpha-HCP material and brittle oxides.
Water quenching from 1300-1400°C at more than 100°C/s suppresses diffusion-controlled alpha-HCP nucleation and retains metastable single-phase beta-BCC HfNbTaTiZr.
Cooling below 10°C/s will permit alpha-HCP formation.
The proposed process will yield greater than 98% theoretical density.
The quenched alloy will have a single-phase beta-BCC crystal structure with no detectable alpha-HCP or alpha-Ti.
The quenched microstructure will have a grain size of 1-5 µm because rapid cooling limits structural coarsening.
The resulting alloy will exhibit a hardness of approximately HV 400-500 and moderate ductility.
Sintering in air or low-purity argon without a getter will produce a porous, oxygen-embrittled, dual- or multiphase microstructure.
Absence of HCP diffraction peaks around 2θ = 35-40° using Cu Kα radiation can establish the absence of alpha-Ti or other alpha-HCP phases.
Detection of alpha-HCP during cooling or more than 10% non-beta-BCC secondary phases after cooling would falsify the predicted phase outcome.

contradictions.description: The grain-size rationale invokes rapid solidification, but the specified process is solid-state sintering followed by quenching and does not identify any melting or solidification step.

The mechanism attributes limited grain growth partly to a lack of prolonged high-temperature exposure, while the regime specifies a 30-60 minute hold at 1300-1400°C, which is substantial high-temperature exposure and requires justification.
